chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.html:
In Quebec, the landlord-tenant relationship is governed by precise rules and by the Rental Tribunal (TAL). Knowing them means avoiding conflicts, costly mistakes, and unpleasant surprises.

This guide covers the lease, tenant selection, rent increases, each party's rights and obligations, and the role of the TAL.

Informational content, not legal advice. Each chapter ends with a lined « My notes » page.

chapters.title: The lease and tenant selection
chapters.html:
Start on solid ground.

The lease (often the official TAL form) sets the terms of the tenancy: rent, term, conditions, building rules. Rigorous tenant selection is your best protection against problems.

  • Check references and payment history (within the bounds of the law).
  • Complete a clear and thorough lease.
  • Provide the mandatory documents and the building rules, where applicable.
Emilie's tip

A good, well-chosen tenant is worth more than a unit rented quickly and carelessly. Take the time to select: it is your best insurance against unpaid rent and conflicts.

chapters.title: The rent increase
chapters.objective: Increase rent correctly, within the rules.
chapters.html:
Increase rent correctly, within the rules.

A rent increase is regulated: it is done at lease renewal, with notice within the required timeframes, and the tenant has the right to refuse it. In the event of disagreement, the amount can be set by the TAL, which applies criteria (expenses, work, etc.).

  • Respect the notice periods for an increase.
  • Justify the increase (rises in taxes, insurance, major work).
  • Know that the tenant can refuse and that the TAL can decide.
Emilie's tip

Never improvise an increase « by feel ». Respect the deadlines and document your justifications: that is what holds up if the file goes to the TAL.

chapters.title: Each party's rights and obligations
chapters.objective: Know the framework to avoid disputes.
chapters.html:
Know the framework to avoid disputes.

  • Landlord: provide a unit in good condition, carry out necessary repairs, respect the tenant's peaceful enjoyment of the premises.
  • Tenant: pay the rent on time, maintain the unit, respect the rules.
  • Access to the unit: the landlord must follow notice rules to visit or carry out work.

Most conflicts arise from a lack of awareness of these rules on both sides. Knowing them saves you a great deal of trouble.

Emilie's tip

Scrupulously respect the rules on access to the unit. Entering without proper notice is a common mistake that can put you in the wrong, even for a good reason.

chapters.title: The role of the TAL
chapters.objective: Understand the tribunal that settles disputes.
chapters.html:
Understand the tribunal that settles disputes.

The Rental Tribunal (TAL) settles disputes between landlords and tenants: rent setting, non-payment, repossession of a unit, repairs, lease termination, etc. You file an application, and the tribunal renders a decision.

Documenting your files well (leases, notices, communications, proof of payment or of work) is essential if you have to go before the TAL.

Emilie's tip

Document everything, all the time: leases, notices, exchanges, invoices. At the TAL, the party with written evidence is in a far stronger position than the one recounting from memory.

chapters.title: Action plan
chapters.html:
Your next steps, in concrete terms.

This week

  1. Put in place a rigorous selection process.
  2. Use a clear and compliant lease.

Within 30 days

  1. Systematically document notices, communications, and invoices.
  2. Learn about the increase deadlines and the access rules.

Then

  1. Consult as needed on a proceeding before the TAL, files in hand.

chapters.title: Resources & glossary
chapters.html:
• TAL: the Rental Tribunal, which settles rental disputes.
  • Lease: the tenancy contract, often the official TAL form.
  • Notice of increase: a notification governed by deadlines.
  • Peaceful enjoyment: the tenant's right to the quiet use of the unit.
  • Access rules: the notice conditions for visiting or carrying out work.

qcm.q: In Quebec, rental disputes are settled by:
qcm.explanation: The TAL is the competent tribunal (ch. 4).

qcm.q: The best protection against problems is:

options: B) At renewal, with notice within the deadlines
B) Refuse the increase, with the TAL able to decide

qcm.q: The landlord must, among other things:
options: B) Provide a unit in good condition and respect peaceful enjoyment

qcm.q: To visit or carry out work, the landlord must:
Before the TAL, the major asset is:

options: B) A lack of awareness of the rules on both sides
